title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: A great business is one that can reinvest large amounts of incremental capital at high rates of return—and return the rest without ego.
epigraph.author: Institutional Quality Principle

web_blocks.html: Over the ten fiscal years from FY2017 to FY2026, Costco more than doubled its revenue base [6, 7, 11]. Total revenue climbed from $129,025 million to $303,154 million, a 9.96% compound annual growth rate [6, 7, 11]. That pace held firm across a global pandemic, a 40-year inflation spike, and shifting tariff regimes [6, 7, 11]. Operating income grew even faster, rising from $4,111 million in FY2017 to $11,685 million in FY2026 [7, 11]. That equals a 12.31% CAGR as operating margin expanded by 66 basis points from 3.19% to 3.85% [7, 11].

The quality of that margin expansion stands out just as much. Gross margin on net sales stayed inside a tight 10.48% to 11.13% band across the entire decade [6]. Costco never broke its cost-plus promise to members [6]. Instead, operating leverage came from lower SG&A costs and steady membership fee growth [6, 7]. SG&A dropped from ~10.0% of sales in FY2017 to 9.15% of net sales in FY2026 [6, 7]. Meanwhile, membership fees compounded at an 8.42% CAGR from $2,853 million to $5,907 million [6, 7]. Net income compounded at 14.72% per year, rising from $2,679 million in FY2017 to $9,226 million in FY2026 [7, 11].

web_blocks.caption: Costco 10-Year Financial Forensics (FY2017–FY2026, $ Millions)
web_blocks.takeaway: From FY2017 to FY2026, Total Revenue grew at ~10.0% CAGR, Operating Income at ~12.3% CAGR, and Net Income at ~14.7% CAGR. Costco achieved that growth without ever breaching its ~11% merchandise gross margin cap.

web_blocks.html: Costco's cash conversion ranks among the best in global retail. In FY2026, Cash Flow from Operations (CFO) hit $15,825 million, up 18.7% YoY from $13,335 million in FY2025 [7]. That cash flow equaled 171.5% of GAAP Net Income ($9,226 million) [7]. Capital spending totaled $6,435 million, mostly for owned warehouse builds, remodels, and depots [7]. Free Cash Flow still reached $9,390 million, or 101.8% of Net Income [7]. Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) hit 21.23%, Return on Equity (ROE) hit 28.40%, and Return on Assets (ROA) stood at 11.11% [26].

At August 30, 2026, Costco held $20,207 million in cash and equivalents plus $1,094 million in short-term investments [7]. Total liquidity stood at $21,301 million against $6,162 million in total debt ($2,248 million current plus $3,914 million long-term) [7]. Long-term operating lease liabilities added just $2,414 million [7]. That left ~$15.1 billion in net cash (ex-leases) and a low 0.28x Debt/Equity ratio [7, 26]. On November 10, 2026, the board declared a ~$13.3 billion ($30/share) special cash dividend payable December 4, 2026 [16, 27]. It marks the sixth special payout after $7 (2012), $5 (2015), $7 (2017), $10 (2020), and $15 (Jan 2024) [16, 27]. Even after that payout, the balance sheet stays net-cash positive and self-funds the ~$7.5 billion FY2027 capex plan [16, 27].

web_blocks.title: 6.3 ROIC Decomposition, ASC 842 Leases & Working-Capital Float Durability

web_blocks.html: Breaking down Costco's 21.23% ROIC into DuPont drivers shows why rivals struggle to copy its moat [7, 26]. ROIC equals NOPAT margin times invested-capital turnover [7, 26]. On $303,154 million of FY2026 revenue and $11,685 million of operating income (3.85% margin), a 24%–25% tax rate leaves ~$8.8 billion to $8.9 billion in NOPAT [7]. That works out to a thin ~2.9% after-tax operating margin [7]. Most retailers with a sub-3% NOPAT margin fail to beat their cost of capital. Costco clears its hurdle nearly threefold because it turns invested capital over 7.2x per year [6, 7]. Rapid inventory velocity (~12x annual turns) and a negative working-capital cycle drive that speed [6, 7].

Two balance-sheet traits strengthen that edge, though automated screens often miss them. First, under ASC 842 lease rules, Costco holds only $2,414 million in long-term operating lease debt across 939 stores [1, 7]. It owns 94.9% of its buildings and ~81% of its land, avoiding landlord rent hikes and lease friction [7]. Even if we count all operating leases alongside $6,162 million of funded debt, $21,301 million of cash still leaves ~$12.7 billion net cash [7]. Second, Costco's working-capital float is built to last [7, 18]. Suppliers are paid after goods sell for cash, while $5,907 million in annual fees arrive upfront as deferred revenue [7, 18]. That float explains why FY2026 CFO ($15,825 million) beat net income ($9,226 million) by $6,599 million—a 171.5% conversion rate that funds both ~$7.5 billion in FY2027 capex and special dividends [7, 16].

web_blocks.caption: Costco Capital Efficiency, Lease Ownership & Float Forensics (FY2026)
rows: Thin cost-plus margin multiplied by extreme asset velocity [7, 26].
Minimal lease leverage; net cash remains ~$12.7B even after adding LT leases [7].
Supplier payables + upfront deferred fees fund inventory before cash leaves [7, 18].
web_blocks.takeaway: Costco earns 21.23% ROIC from 7.3x capital turnover, 94.9% owned buildings, and negative working-capital float [7, 19, 26]. That engine funds $13.3B in special dividends without hurting store capex [7, 19, 26].

book_paragraphs: When you lay Costco's ten-year income statement on the table from FY2017 through FY2026, the first thing that jumps out is not a flashy spike—it is the eerie, clockwork consistency of the compounding. Total revenue grew from $129.0 billion in FY2017 to $303.2 billion in FY2026, a 10.0% annual compound rate across a decade that threw everything from a global pandemic to 9% inflation and tariff upheaval at the retail sector. Operating income compounded at 12.3% a year, from $4.11 billion to $11.69 billion, and net income compounded at 14.7% a year, from $2.68 billion to $9.23 billion.

How does a retailer grow earnings nearly 50% faster than sales for a decade without raising its merchandise gross margin? Look at the gross margin band: 10.48% to 11.13% every single year. Costco never broke its promise to the member. Instead, it squeezed SG&A down from roughly 10% of sales in FY2017 to 9.15% of net sales in FY2026, while membership fee income compounded from $2.85 billion to $5.91 billion.

Before you and I leave the financial statements, let us look underneath that 21.23% Return on Invested Capital, because the math explains why competitors cannot simply copy Costco's playbook. Every ROIC figure is the product of two levers: how much after-tax profit you keep on each dollar of sales (NOPAT margin), and how many times a year you spin each dollar of invested capital (capital turnover). On $303.2 billion of revenue and $11.69 billion of operating income, Costco's after-tax operating margin is right around 2.9%. In almost any other physical business, a 2.9% NOPAT margin would produce mediocre returns. Costco turns it into a 21.23% ROIC by spinning its invested capital more than seven times a year. Goods arrive at the depot, move onto pallets, and sell for cash or debit before the supplier invoice even comes due.

Notice what that negative working-capital float does for you as an owner. Most growing retailers have to tie up billions of dollars in inventory and store fixtures just to open new locations, so growth consumes cash. At Costco, growth generates cash. Add in $5.91 billion of annual membership fees collected upfront—sitting on the balance sheet as deferred revenue before a single item is scanned—and you see why Cash Flow from Operations hit $15,825 million in FY2026 against $9,226 million of GAAP net income. That extra $6.60 billion of annual operating cash flow is not an accounting trick; it is the structural float of a membership warehouse.

book_subsections.title: Cash Conversion, ROIC & Special-Dividend Discipline
paragraphs: Now turn to the cash flow statement, because that is where Costco separates itself from ordinary retailers. In FY2026, GAAP net income was $9,226 million, yet Cash Flow from Operations hit $15,825 million—171.5% cash conversion. Even after pouring $6,435 million back into new warehouses, depots, and remodels, Costco generated $9,390 million in Free Cash Flow, or 101.8% of net income. That is how a brick-and-mortar retailer achieves a 21.23% Return on Invested Capital and a 28.40% Return on Equity while owning nearly 95% of its store buildings.

Finally, look at the August 30, 2026 balance sheet: $21.3 billion in cash and short-term investments against just $6.16 billion in total debt, leaving roughly $15.1 billion in net cash before operating leases. Costco has consistently refused to hoard idle cash or chase ego-driven acquisitions. Instead, whenever cash piles up beyond what its 30-warehouse-per-year capex pipeline can absorb, the board sends it back in a lump sum—$7 in 2012, $5 in 2015, $7 in 2017, $10 in 2020, $15 in January 2024, and $30 per share (~$13.3 billion) declared on November 10, 2026. Purely on business fundamentals, Costco is a textbook compounder.

book_subsections.title: ASC 842 Lease Accounting, Owned Real Estate & Special-Dividend Cadence
paragraphs: Another place where a careful forensic reader separates Costco from the retail pack is lease accounting. Under ASC 842, companies must capitalize their long-term store leases onto the balance sheet. If you pull up a typical big-box or specialty retailer, you will often see massive operating lease liabilities dwarfing funded debt, because the retailer rents 70% or 80% of its stores and faces relentless rent escalations every five years. On Costco's August 30, 2026 balance sheet, long-term operating lease liabilities total just $2,414 million—a rounding error relative to $303.2 billion in sales. Why? Because Costco owns 94.9% of its warehouse buildings and roughly 81% of the land beneath them. Even if you treat every penny of those ASC 842 lease obligations as debt alongside $6,162 million of funded debt, Costco's $21.3 billion cash and short-term investment pile still leaves roughly $12.7 billion of net cash.

That brings us to Costco's signature capital-return habit: the special cash dividend. Most corporate boards prefer either creeping up the regular dividend or running steady share buybacks regardless of business cycles. Costco's board takes a far more disciplined, owner-oriented approach. It funds its ~30-warehouse-per-year expansion first—stepping capex up from $6.44 billion in FY2026 to roughly $7.5 billion in FY2027—and keeps a fortress liquidity cushion for operational flexibility. Then, every two to four years when excess cash accumulates beyond what new warehouses can absorb, it hands the surplus back in a clean lump sum: $7 per share in 2012, $5 in 2015, $7 in 2017, $10 in 2020, $15 in January 2024, and now $30 per share—roughly $13.3 billion—declared on November 10, 2026. Even after wiring out $13.3 billion in December, Costco remains net-cash positive and fully self-funding. On pure business quality and balance-sheet stewardship, there is nothing left to criticize.

There is one more strategic dividend from owning 94.9% of those warehouse buildings that never shows up as a separate line on the income statement: inflation protection and permanent site control. When a traditional grocer or big-box chain leases its stores, a landlord captures the upside of neighborhood population growth every time a ten-year lease renews. Because Costco owns both the building and roughly 81% of the land beneath it, its occupancy cost stays anchored in historical cost while its sales per square foot climb year after year. Look at the resulting return profile: 21.23% ROIC, 28.40% ROE, and 11.11% ROA, achieved with a tiny 0.28x Debt-to-Equity ratio and zero financial engineering. You and I could not design a cleaner capital structure on a whiteboard.

book_callouts.title: The Quality Verdict on Fundamentals Alone
book_callouts.text: Before you ever look at a stock's price, ask whether the underlying machine passes the quality gate: 10% ten-year revenue CAGR, 14.7% net income CAGR, 171.5% CFO conversion, 21.2% ROIC, 92.3% North American renewal, and a net-cash balance sheet. On business quality alone, Costco is an unambiguous Compounder Pass.
